nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career phases: the 1980s Italo-disco breakthrough, the documented 1992–1999 break, and the later reunion ending in 2016. The gap is inactivity, not a measured popularity threshold; shades are approximate.

nodes.name: Robert Hood
nodes.description: Detroit techno producer and DJ; co-founded Underground Resistance before establishing the stripped-down solo sound heard on Minimal Nation (1994), a landmark in minimal techno.

nodes.name: Robert Johnson
nodes.description: Delta blues singer and guitarist whose small recorded catalogue became influential in later blues and rock.

nodes.name: Robert Miles
nodes.description: Swiss-Italian DJ and producer whose piano-led “Children” helped define the 1990s dream-trance sound.

nodes.name: The Rolling Stones
nodes.description: English rock band formed in 1962, rooted in Chicago blues and still recording in 2026; their long career spans major changes in members and sound.

nodes.name: Romeo Santos
nodes.description: American singer-songwriter who first recorded as a teenager with Los Tinellers, later became Aventura’s lead singer and helped bring bachata to a global audience, then launched a solo career in 2011.

nodes.name: Ron Hardy
nodes.description: Chicago DJ and producer whose raw, high-energy Music Box sets helped shape house music; he repeatedly played Phuture’s “Acid Tracks” from cassette, helping establish its reputation.

nodes.name: Ron Trent
nodes.description: Chicago house DJ and producer whose deep, expansive productions and Prescription label helped shape 1990s deep house.

nodes.name: Roni Size
nodes.description: Bristol drum-and-bass producer and DJ, best known for leading Reprazent and blending programmed rhythms with live musicians.

nodes.name: RP Boo
nodes.description: Chicago producer, DJ and former dancer Kavain Space, known as RP Boo, whose “Baby Come On” (1997) is widely cited as a foundational footwork track.

nodes.name: Run-DMC
nodes.description: Queens hip-hop trio whose sparse, forceful sound and rock crossovers helped move rap into album and mainstream rock audiences; the group ended after Jam Master Jay’s 2002 death.

nodes.name: The Sabri Brothers
nodes.description: Pakistani qawwali ensemble formed around brothers Ghulam Farid Sabri and Maqbool Ahmed Sabri, renowned for bringing Sufi devotional singing to international audiences.

nodes.name: Saint Vitus
nodes.description: Los Angeles doom metal band first formed as Tyrant in 1979, adopting the Saint Vitus name by 1981; their slow, heavy sound became foundational to doom metal.

nodes.name: Sam Cooke
nodes.description: American singer, songwriter and entrepreneur whose gospel career with the Soul Stirrers began around 1950–51. His 1956 secular recordings and 1957 hit “You Send Me” helped bridge gospel vocal practice and postwar pop and soul. He founded SAR Records and wrote “A Change Is Gonna Come” before his death in 1964.

nodes.name: Savage
nodes.description: Italian singer and songwriter Roberto Zanetti, whose 1983 single “Don’t Cry Tonight” became a defining Italo disco hit.

nodes.name: Arnold Schoenberg
nodes.description: Austrian-American composer and theorist whose path from late Romanticism through free atonality to the twelve-tone method reshaped twentieth-century music.

nodes.name: Scientist
nodes.description: Jamaican dub producer and recording engineer Hopeton Brown, known as Scientist, who developed his mixing craft at King Tubby’s studio and became a prominent dub artist around 1980.

nodes.name: Selena
nodes.description: Tejano singer Selena Quintanilla began performing as a child with her family band Selena y Los Dinos; her 1990s success helped bring Tejano and Latin pop to wider U.S. audiences.

nodes.name: Sex Pistols
nodes.description: English punk band that became a defining force in the 1976–78 UK punk surge; later reunions and a 2025 touring lineup make the group’s overall activity open-ended.

nodes.name: Shabba Ranks
nodes.description: Jamaican dancehall deejay whose forceful digital-era style and crossover hits helped introduce dancehall to international and U.S. audiences.

nodes.name: Shang Xiaoyun
nodes.description: Chinese Peking opera performer and teacher, one of the “Four Great Dan” actors, celebrated for developing the Shang school of performance.

nodes.name: Showtek
nodes.description: Dutch duo of brothers Wouter and Sjoerd Janssen, leading hardstyle producers in the 2000s who crossed over to mainstream EDM in the 2010s and returned to hardstyle in 2023.

nodes.name: Shy FX
nodes.description: London jungle and drum-and-bass producer Andre Williams, known as Shy FX, whose 1994 “Original Nuttah” became a defining ragga-jungle track.

nodes.name: Skepta
nodes.description: North London grime MC, DJ and producer whose pirate-radio and crew roots led to solo albums, the Boy Better Know collective and a wider international audience for grime.

nodes.name: Skream
nodes.description: South London producer and DJ Oliver Jones, known as Skream, was an early dubstep innovator whose 2005 “Midnight Request Line” became a defining track before he moved into house, disco and techno.

nodes.name: SL2
nodes.description: English rave duo Slipmatt and Lime, with MC Jay J, whose 1989 releases and 1992 hit “On a Ragga Tip” bridged breakbeat hardcore and chart pop.

nodes.name: Slayer
nodes.description: California thrash metal band formed in 1981, noted for extreme speed and dark subject matter; after a 2019 farewell tour, the band resumed live performances in 2024.

nodes.name: Sleep
nodes.description: San Jose doom metal band whose slow, heavy riffs and long-form songs shaped stoner metal; after a late-1990s breakup, Sleep reunited and resumed recording and touring.

nodes.name: Slint
nodes.description: Louisville rock band whose angular arrangements and dynamic, spoken-word passages on Tweez and Spiderland became major reference points for post-rock and indie rock.

nodes.name: Slipknot
nodes.description: Des Moines heavy metal band formed in 1995; its masked nine-member lineup and aggressive blend of extreme metal and percussion drove a major mainstream breakthrough with the 1999 debut.

nodes.name: Slowdive
nodes.description: Reading shoegaze band formed in 1989, known for layered guitar textures and hazy vocals; after reuniting in 2014, the group resumed recording and touring.

nodes.name: Sly and the Family Stone
nodes.description: San Francisco band led by Sly Stone that fused soul, funk and rock, with Larry Graham’s percussive bass shaping early funk. The original lineup’s last album was Small Talk (1974); Stone kept the name until the early 1980s.

nodes.name: Snoop Dogg
nodes.description: Long Beach rapper and producer whose 1992 introduction on Dr. Dre’s The Chronic led to the 1993 G-funk landmark Doggystyle and a long-running career across music and media.

nodes.name: So Solid Crew
nodes.description: South London UK garage and hip-hop collective whose large rotating membership and 2001 chart-topper “21 Seconds” brought the scene into the mainstream.

nodes.name: Sonic Youth
nodes.description: New York experimental rock band formed in 1981, known for alternate guitar tunings, noise and exploratory composition; the group entered an indefinite hiatus after its final 2011 performance.

nodes.name: The Sonics
nodes.description: Tacoma garage rock band founded around 1960, whose raw, distorted recordings such as “The Witch” and Here Are the Sonics!!! influenced punk and garage revival bands.

nodes.name: Soundgarden
nodes.description: Seattle band combining heavy riffs, unusual meters and a wide vocal range; after disbanding in 2017 following Chris Cornell’s death, surviving members have performed intermittently and are completing an album featuring his recordings.

nodes.name: Squarepusher
nodes.description: English electronic musician Tom Jenkinson, known for combining intricate drum programming, jazz-influenced bass playing and experimental electronics.

nodes.name: Stacey Pullen
nodes.description: Detroit techno DJ and producer associated with the second wave of the scene.

nodes.name: Steve Reich
nodes.description: American composer and pioneer of minimalism, known for phasing, repeating patterns and gradual musical processes.

nodes.name: Igor Stravinsky
nodes.description: Russian-born composer whose work moved through Russian-period ballets, neoclassicism and serial music; the 1966 endpoint marks his last completed composition, not his death in 1971.

nodes.name: Suede
nodes.description: London alternative rock band formed in 1989; their 1992–93 breakthrough helped launch Britpop, and later albums show a sustained return after their 2000s hiatus.

nodes.name: Sunny Day Real Estate
nodes.description: Seattle emo and alternative rock band formed in 1992; Diary (1994) became a touchstone of second-wave emo. Reunions and later tours make the career intermittent, not a continuous 1994–present run.

nodes.name: Sven Väth
nodes.description: German DJ and producer who helped shape Frankfurt’s electronic music scene through residencies, club promotion and labels including Eye Q and Harthouse.

nodes.name: Swedish House Mafia
nodes.description: Swedish electronic dance music trio of Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso. The group coalesced in 2008, reached international pop-dance success in the early 2010s, announced a farewell period in 2013, reunited in 2018 and released its debut studio album Paradise Again in 2022.

nodes.name: Sylvester
nodes.description: American disco and Hi-NRG singer whose gospel-rooted voice and gender-bending stage presence made him a major queer music icon; he died of AIDS-related illness in 1988.

nodes.name: T. Rex
nodes.description: English rock project led by Marc Bolan, founded as the acoustic duo Tyrannosaurus Rex in 1967 and renamed T. Rex as its sound turned electric around 1970; ended with Bolan’s death in 1977.

nodes.name: Tabu Ley Rochereau
nodes.description: Congolese singer-songwriter and bandleader who began with African Jazz in 1959 and became a central voice in Congolese rumba and soukous.

nodes.name: Talking Heads
nodes.description: New York art rock band combining punk-era independence with funk, African polyrhythms and studio experimentation; officially ended in 1991 after an influential run.

nodes.name: Tangerine Dream
nodes.description: Berlin group founded by Edgar Froese in 1967. After early tape-collage krautrock, sequencer albums such as Phaedra (1974) defined a spacey electronic style influential on ambient and electronic music; the group continued after Froese’s death in 2015.

nodes.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
nodes.description: Russian Romantic composer of symphonies, operas, concertos and ballets; he began professional musical work after leaving the civil service and studying at the St. Petersburg Conservatory.

nodes.name: Teddy Riley
nodes.description: American record producer and songwriter credited with creating new jack swing, blending R&B vocals, hip-hop rhythms and electronic production; later led the groups Guy and Blackstreet.

nodes.name: Terry Riley
nodes.description: American composer and performer whose 1964 In C helped establish minimalism through repeating musical cells that performers can play in flexible alignment.

nodes.name: The Beach Boys
nodes.description: California vocal group founded in Hawthorne in 1961; their close harmonies and Brian Wilson’s studio innovations shaped surf pop and ambitious 1960s rock. The touring name continues with a different lineup.

nodes.name: The Beatles
nodes.description: Liverpool band whose songwriting and studio experiments reshaped rock and pop.

nodes.name: The Clash
nodes.description: British punk band that fused punk with reggae, dub, ska, rockabilly and funk; the original group disbanded in 1986 after a decade of rapid musical development.

nodes.name: The Coasters
nodes.description: Los Angeles vocal group formed in 1955 from members of the Robins, known for comic Leiber–Stoller story songs set to doo-wop and R&B grooves. Later touring lineups continue the name.

nodes.name: The Cure
nodes.description: English band that began as Easy Cure in 1976 and adopted the name The Cure in 1978; their catalogue ranges from stark post-punk and gothic textures to melodic pop, with recording activity continuing into the 2020s.

nodes.name: The Drifters
nodes.description: New York vocal group formed in 1953 around Clyde McPhatter whose shifting lineups, later with Ben E. King and Johnny Moore, recorded R&B hits such as “There Goes My Baby” (1959). Successor lineups continue to perform.

nodes.name: The Heptones
nodes.description: Jamaican vocal trio formed in Kingston and closely associated with Studio One, whose three-part harmonies carried rocksteady into reggae.

nodes.name: The Human League
nodes.description: Sheffield electronic pop group formed in 1977, initially built around synthesizers and experimental performance; a major 1980 lineup change preceded their synth-pop breakthrough.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence centered on Dare in 1981, Human in 1986, and the mid-1990s Tell Me When return. Later activity remains visible; the shades are an approximate interpretation of recording eras rather than a popularity series.

nodes.name: The Orb
nodes.description: English electronic music project led by Alex Paterson, known for ambient house and expansive, sample-based productions; collaborators and lineup have changed over time.

nodes.name: The Platters
nodes.description: Los Angeles vocal group whose crooning ballads such as “Only You” (1955) and “Smoke Gets in Your Eyes” (1958) carried doo-wop to the pop charts. Later lineups continue to tour.

nodes.name: The Prodigy
nodes.description: English electronic music group formed around Liam Howlett’s rave tracks and live performers in Braintree, Essex. The project emerged from rave and breakbeat-hardcore culture; its first EP appeared in 1991 and Charly became a UK chart breakthrough that year.

nodes.name: The Prophet
nodes.description: Amsterdam DJ and producer (Dov Elkabas), a member of the 1990s gabber Dreamteam and later the founder of the Scantraxx hardstyle label. He played a farewell set at Defqon.1 in 2023.

nodes.name: The Ronettes
nodes.description: New York girl group of Ronnie, Estelle and Nedra, later known for Phil Spector-produced hits including “Be My Baby”; the original group’s run ended in the late 1960s.

nodes.name: The Shangri-Las
nodes.description: Queens girl group known for theatrical, story-driven pop singles such as “Leader of the Pack”; their original run largely ended by 1968.

nodes.name: The Skatalites
nodes.description: Jamaican ska band assembled from leading Kingston studio musicians in 1964; after the original 1964–65 run, successive reunions from 1983 onward kept the group active with a changing lineup.

nodes.name: The Stooges
nodes.description: Ann Arbor rock band formed in 1967 around Iggy Pop and the Asheton brothers; their abrasive, stripped-down sound influenced punk and later alternative rock.

nodes.name: The Supremes
nodes.description: Detroit vocal group formed as the Primettes in 1959 and renamed the Supremes after signing to Motown in 1961; the 1977 end date refers to the group’s disbandment, not Diana Ross’s later solo career.

nodes.name: The Ventures
nodes.description: Tacoma instrumental rock band formed by Don Wilson and Bob Bogle; “Walk, Don’t Run” made them international stars and helped define surf rock guitar.

nodes.name: The Who
nodes.description: British rock band known for forceful live performance, ambitious songwriting, and rock operas such as Tommy. It split in 1983 and has worked again, with reunions, since the late 1980s.

nodes.name: Thelonious Monk
nodes.description: American jazz pianist and composer whose angular melodies, unexpected silences and distinctive harmonies helped shape bebop and modern jazz; his last public appearance was in 1976.

nodes.name: Theo Parrish
nodes.description: Detroit house DJ, producer and label founder whose soulful, jazz- and disco-informed sound and long, eclectic sets became central to the city’s underground scene.

nodes.name: T.I.
nodes.description: Atlanta rapper Clifford “T.I.” Harris, an early architect of trap’s mainstream rise, who began rapping as a child, signed his first major label deal in 1999 and released his debut album in 2001.

nodes.name: Tito Puente
nodes.description: New York timbalero, vibraphonist and bandleader, the “King of Mambo” of the Palladium era and one of the leading figures in Latin jazz.

nodes.name: Todd Terry
nodes.description: Brooklyn house producer and DJ whose fast, sample-heavy productions bridged house and hip-hop and helped shape New York club music in the late 1980s.

nodes.name: Tony Allen
nodes.description: Nigerian drummer, composer and bandleader. He played with Fela Kuti from 1964 to 1979 and was a central co-creator of Afrobeat’s rhythmic language; after leaving Africa 70, he led his own groups and built an international career across jazz, funk and electronic collaborations.
nodes.phaseNote: Allen played highlife in Lagos before his documented 1964–79 collaboration with Fela Kuti, and later pursued an independent career. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Toots & the Maytals
nodes.description: Jamaican vocal group led by Toots Hibbert, whose gospel-inflected singing bridged ska, rocksteady and reggae; the group’s main career ended with his death in 2020.

nodes.name: Tricky
nodes.description: Bristol artist Adrian Thaws, a former Wild Bunch and Massive Attack collaborator whose 1995 solo debut Maxinquaye became a landmark of trip-hop.

nodes.name: Trouble
nodes.description: Chicago doom metal band formed in 1979; Psalm 9 (1984) and The Skull (1985) established its slow, heavy sound, and the group continues to perform and prepare new music.

nodes.name: Tujamo
nodes.description: German DJ and producer Matthias Richter, known as Tujamo, who began producing under the alias in 2006 and had his first major international hit with “Boneless” in 2013.

nodes.name: Tunde Nightingale
nodes.description: Nigerian juju singer and bandleader who helped establish the genre’s recognizable postwar sound and introduced the shekere into juju ensembles.

nodes.name: Tupac Shakur
nodes.description: American rapper and actor whose socially conscious writing, forceful delivery and varied personas made him one of hip-hop’s central figures; his professional recording career ran from 1991 until his murder in 1996.

nodes.name: U. Srinivas
nodes.description: Carnatic mandolinist who adapted the electric mandolin to South Indian classical music from childhood and later worked in cross-cultural projects such as Remember Shakti.

nodes.name: UGK
nodes.description: Port Arthur, Texas rap duo Bun B and Pimp C, central to Southern hip-hop; their final album, UGK 4 Life, was completed and released after Pimp C’s 2007 death.

nodes.name: Umm Kulthum
nodes.description: Egyptian singer whose long-form performances joined poetic texts with Arabic musical practice and reached audiences across the Arab world through recordings, radio and touring.

nodes.name: Uncle Tupelo
nodes.description: Belleville, Illinois alternative-country band whose punk energy and country songwriting helped shape alt-country; its 1994 breakup led to the formation of Wilco and Son Volt.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit music collective and record label whose releases linked techno production with independent infrastructure and political expression. Its contributors and roster changed over time; anonymity and collective presentation are recurring parts of its public identity.

nodes.name: Hikaru Utada
nodes.description: Japanese-American singer-songwriter whose 1998 Japanese-language debut “Automatic/time will tell” made her a major pop star; she has continued releasing albums and performing through the 2020s.

nodes.name: Vasily Andreyev
nodes.description: Russian balalaika virtuoso, composer and bandleader who popularized the instrument in concert settings and organized a Russian folk-instrument orchestra.

nodes.name: Venetian Snares
nodes.description: Canadian electronic musician Aaron Funk, known for intricately programmed breakcore, extreme rhythmic shifts and unexpected melodic material.

nodes.name: Antonio Vivaldi
nodes.description: Venetian Baroque composer and violinist, especially associated with the solo concerto.

nodes.name: Warren G
nodes.description: Long Beach rapper and producer whose smooth G-funk production and 1994 hit “Regulate” helped bring West Coast hip-hop to a wide audience; he had earlier formed 213 with Snoop Dogg and Nate Dogg.

nodes.name: Washed Out
nodes.description: Georgia electronic musician Ernest Greene, whose bedroom-produced 2009 Life of Leisure EP and “Feel It All Around” helped define the early chillwave sound.

nodes.name: Weather Report
nodes.description: Electric jazz-fusion group founded by Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter.

nodes.name: Wildstylez
nodes.description: Dutch hardstyle DJ and producer Joram Metekohy, half of Project One with Headhunterz, whose “Year of Summer” became the first hardstyle track in the Dutch Top 2000.

nodes.name: William Byrd
nodes.description: English Renaissance composer of sacred polyphony, consort music and keyboard works; his first known professional appointment was organist and choirmaster at Lincoln Cathedral in 1563.

nodes.name: Willie Colón
nodes.description: New York-born trombonist, bandleader, composer and producer central to Fania’s urban salsa sound; his 1967 debut El Malo launched a career that continued across recording, performance and civic work until 2026.

nodes.name: Wizkid
nodes.description: Nigerian singer-songwriter and Afrobeats star Ayodeji Balogun, who began pursuing music full-time in 2006 and broke through across Africa with his 2011 debut album Superstar.

nodes.name: Women on Wax
nodes.description: Detroit-area collective founded by DJ Minx in December 1996 to platform women DJs and singers. It was a collective and event platform before the 2001 launch of Women On Wax Recordings; Minx relaunched the label in 2023.

nodes.name: Yellowman
nodes.description: Jamaican dancehall deejay whose 1979 Tastee Talent Contest win launched his rise and whose early-1980s albums helped bring dancehall to international audiences.

nodes.name: Yes
nodes.description: Progressive-rock group known for extended compositions, virtuoso playing, and changing lineups.

nodes.name: Ying Yang Twins
nodes.description: Atlanta rap duo D-Roc and Kaine, formed in 1997 and known for Southern club rap and call-and-response party singles, including the 2000 breakthrough “Whistle While You Twurk.”

nodes.name: Yo-Yo Ma
nodes.description: American cellist born in Paris, celebrated for classical performances and collaborations across musical traditions; he began studying cello at four and gave his first public recital at five.

nodes.name: RCA Victor introduces the 45 rpm single
nodes.description: RCA Victor introduced the 45 rpm record in 1949, intensifying competition among disc formats and supporting the single as a durable unit of popular-music release.

nodes.name: AFM recording ban ends for major labels
nodes.description: By late 1944, settlements with major record companies ended the American Federation of Musicians’ recording ban. The dispute helped bring royalty payments for musicians’ recorded work into industry negotiations.

nodes.name: AFM recording ban begins
nodes.description: The American Federation of Musicians began a recording ban in 1942 amid disputes over payments for recorded music. The action interrupted commercial recording by union members and continued on different terms across companies into 1944.

nodes.name: Alam Ara introduces song-led Indian sound cinema
nodes.description: Ardeshir Irani’s Alam Ara, screened in Bombay on 14 March 1931, is recognized as the first Indian sound film. Its songs helped establish music as a central feature of Indian popular cinema.

nodes.name: Ars nova notation expands rhythmic possibilities
nodes.description: The Ars nova treatise associated with Philippe de Vitry reflects a fourteenth-century shift toward more precisely measured rhythms and increasingly differentiated note values.

nodes.name: Ars subtilior pushes late-medieval notation
nodes.description: Late-fourteenth-century composers developed highly intricate rhythmic notation and composition now grouped under the scholarly term ars subtilior. The date marks an approximate period, not a single founding event.

nodes.name: Baul devotional songs appear in Bengali literature
nodes.description: UNESCO traces Baul devotional songs to the fifteenth century, when they first appeared in Bengali literature. This is a documentary reference point, not a claim that the living tradition began then.

nodes.name: The Beatles perform on The Ed Sullivan Show
nodes.description: The Beatles’ appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964 reached a mass U.S. television audience and accelerated the group’s U.S. breakthrough and the British Invasion.

nodes.name: Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony premieres
nodes.description: The Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna on 7 May 1824. Its choral finale expanded the symphony’s public and expressive possibilities and became one of the most widely recognized works in the concert tradition.

nodes.name: Benny Goodman’s Carnegie Hall concert is recorded
nodes.description: Benny Goodman’s 16 January 1938 Carnegie Hall concert brought swing to a prominent concert venue and was recorded, with the later release helping preserve the performance’s place in jazz history.

nodes.name: Berliner patents the gramophone
nodes.description: Emile Berliner patented a lateral-groove recording system in 1887. He developed it into a flat-disc gramophone that later made commercially successful disc records possible.

nodes.name: Billboard launches the Hot 100
nodes.description: Billboard’s Hot 100 debuted in August 1958, combining sales, radio airplay, and other measures into a national singles chart that became an influential industry reference.

nodes.name: The Bristol Sessions record Appalachian performers
nodes.description: Victor’s Bristol sessions took place in Tennessee in July and August 1927. They recorded performers including the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers and became a watershed in the commercial history of country music.

nodes.name: Kool Herc hosts a Bronx back-to-school party
nodes.description: At a back-to-school party organized with his sister Cindy Campbell on 11 August 1973, DJ Kool Herc used extended break sections to keep dancers moving. The gathering is often cited as a foundational moment in hip-hop, while the culture developed through a wider community and many events.

nodes.name: Cairo hosts the first Congress of Arab Music
nodes.description: Convened under King Fuad I, the congress brought musicians and scholars together in Cairo from 28 March to 3 April to document and debate Arab musical practices. BnF preserves recordings made for the gathering.

nodes.name: Philips introduces the compact cassette
nodes.description: Philips introduced the compact cassette in 1963. The small format later enabled inexpensive home recording, portable listening, and music exchange outside the record industry.

nodes.name: Compact discs enter the consumer market
nodes.description: Sony launched the CDP-101 and CBS/Sony released an initial catalog of compact discs in Japan in October 1982. The format, jointly developed with Philips, reached additional markets in 1983.

nodes.name: Congolese rumba emerges in the Congo cities
nodes.description: In Léopoldville (now Kinshasa) and Brazzaville, Congolese musicians developed an urban style through exchange with imported Cuban recordings and local performance practices. The decade range reflects differing accounts of its early emergence.

nodes.name: Congolese rumba is inscribed by UNESCO
nodes.description: The Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo jointly secured inscription of Congolese rumba on UNESCO’s Representative List, recognizing a living urban music and dance tradition central to Congolese identity and diaspora life.

nodes.name: Council of Trent addresses church music
nodes.description: Across its sessions, the Council of Trent addressed the use and intelligibility of music in Catholic worship. Its discussions formed part of broader Catholic reform; they did not impose one universal ban on polyphony.

nodes.name: COVID-19 closures move live music online
nodes.description: COVID-19 lockdowns and public-health restrictions cancelled or halted live events across many countries. Musicians and institutions shifted concerts and festivals to livestreams, exposing both the reach and limits of digital performance.

nodes.name: Mamie Smith records Crazy Blues
nodes.description: Mamie Smith’s Crazy Blues was recorded and released by Okeh in 1920. Its commercial success helped establish a market for blues records by Black women singers, though it was not the first blues performance or blues recording in history.

nodes.name: Disco Demolition Night erupts in Chicago
nodes.description: A Chicago White Sox promotion on 12 July 1979 invited fans to bring disco records for destruction; the event ended in a field invasion and forfeit. It became a visible episode in the backlash against disco, not the cause of disco’s decline by itself.

nodes.name: Eck Robertson records country music for Victor
nodes.description: Victor recorded fiddler Eck Robertson in 1922, among the earliest commercial records marketed as country or “hillbilly” music. The label is historical and reflects the period’s industry language.

nodes.name: Electrical recording transforms commercial sound
nodes.description: Electrical microphones and amplification entered commercial recording in the mid-1920s, improving fidelity and changing studio practice and the sound of records.

nodes.name: Elvis Presley records at Sun Studio
nodes.description: Elvis Presley’s first Sun recording session in July 1954 produced “That’s All Right,” a key early recording in the emergence and commercial circulation of rock and roll.

nodes.name: Beethoven’s Eroica symphony premieres
nodes.description: Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3, the Eroica, was first performed privately in 1804 and publicly in Vienna in 1805; it enlarged the scale and expressive ambitions of the symphony.

nodes.name: Peri’s Euridice is performed
nodes.description: Jacopo Peri’s Euridice was performed in Florence in 1600. It is the earliest complete opera to survive; Peri’s earlier Dafne (1598) is lost.

nodes.name: Fania All-Stars perform in Kinshasa
nodes.description: The group’s 1974 appearance in Kinshasa carried New York salsa into a major African concert setting; Concord identifies the performance at Stade du Hai and its connection to the film Live in Africa.

nodes.name: Fania All-Stars play Yankee Stadium
nodes.description: The Fania All-Stars’ stadium concert made New York salsa visible on a mass scale and was recorded for the live album released in 1975. Sources differ on whether the concert fell on 23 or 24 August, so the graph records the year only.

nodes.name: Berlioz premieres Symphonie fantastique
nodes.description: Hector Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique premiered in Paris in 1830, using an unusually explicit program and expanded orchestral color to shape a landmark of Romantic symphonic music.

nodes.name: FESTAC ’77 brings African and diasporic arts to Lagos
nodes.description: The Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture took place in Lagos in 1977, presenting music, dance, theatre, and visual arts from across Africa and its diaspora.

nodes.name: Florentine Camerata experiments with dramatic song
nodes.description: A circle of Florentine humanists, poets, and musicians explored monodic song and dramatic music in the late sixteenth century. These experiments contributed to the conditions from which early opera emerged; no single inventor accounts for the genre.

nodes.name: Vivaldi publishes The Four Seasons
nodes.description: Antonio Vivaldi’s concertos later known as The Four Seasons were published in Amsterdam in the collection Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione, Op. 8.

nodes.name: Gangnam Style becomes a global viral music video
nodes.description: PSY’s Gangnam Style became an early global music-video phenomenon on YouTube, demonstrating how online video sharing could propel a Korean-language pop song across national markets.

nodes.name: Commercial gramophone recording sessions begin in Calcutta
nodes.description: Gramophone Company engineer Fred Gaisberg recorded Indian performers in Calcutta in 1902, including Gauhar Jaan. Historians dispute some “first Indian recording” claims, so this event marks a documented recording campaign rather than a definitive first.

nodes.name: The WSM Barn Dance begins broadcasting
nodes.description: The WSM Barn Dance began in Nashville in November 1925 and later became the Grand Ole Opry, a long-running radio institution central to country music’s national circulation.

nodes.name: Grand Upright v. Warner reshapes sample clearance
nodes.description: In Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records, a U.S. federal court ruled against Biz Markie’s uncleared sampling of Gilbert O’Sullivan’s recording. The decision became a prominent warning in debates over sample clearance in hip-hop.

nodes.name: The Great Migration reshapes Black musical life in the United States
nodes.description: The Great Migration moved millions of African Americans from the South to cities across the United States. It created new audiences and networks and reshaped blues, jazz, gospel, and later popular music; music histories describe multiple waves rather than a single date.

nodes.name: Guido of Arezzo systematizes staff notation
nodes.description: Guido of Arezzo’s teaching placed neumes on lines to make pitch relationships easier to read and teach, an important step toward staff notation used in later Western written music.

nodes.name: Hamburg’s public opera house opens
nodes.description: The Oper am Gänsemarkt opened in Hamburg in 1678, extending the commercial public-opera model beyond Italy into a major German-speaking city.

nodes.name: Apple introduces the iPod
nodes.description: Apple introduced the iPod in October 2001, combining portable digital playback with computer-based music libraries and later online purchasing.

nodes.name: iTunes Music Store opens for downloads
nodes.description: Apple launched the iTunes Music Store in the United States on 28 April 2003, selling individual digital tracks through a licensed online store. It helped normalize paid downloads as a mainstream purchase model.

nodes.name: The Jazz Singer brings synchronized song to feature film
nodes.description: The Jazz Singer popularized synchronized dialogue and songs in feature-length cinema in 1927, accelerating the transition from silent film and creating new routes for popular music distribution.

nodes.name: KDKA broadcasts election returns and music
nodes.description: KDKA’s 2 November 1920 broadcast of U.S. election returns is often treated as a milestone in scheduled commercial radio broadcasting. The station also aired music, helping establish radio as a new channel for reaching listeners.

nodes.name: Live Aid broadcasts benefit concerts across continents
nodes.description: Live Aid’s linked benefit concerts in London and Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 used satellite television to connect a global audience and became a landmark of televised benefit performance.

nodes.name: Columbia introduces the 33⅓ rpm LP
nodes.description: Columbia Records introduced its 33⅓ rpm microgroove LP in 1948 in 10-inch and 12-inch editions. The format’s longer playing time let labels fit complete works and longer programs on fewer discs.

nodes.name: Early Lutheran chorales enter print
nodes.description: The first Lutheran hymnals published in 1524 helped circulate congregational chorales in Reformation-era Germany. Printed songbooks became one channel among several through which these repertories spread.

nodes.name: Scott Joplin publishes Maple Leaf Rag
nodes.description: The publication of Scott Joplin’s Maple Leaf Rag helped make ragtime a national sheet-music success and established an enduring model for syncopated piano composition.

nodes.name: Handel’s Messiah premieres in Dublin
nodes.description: Handel’s Messiah received its first public performance in Dublin on 13 April 1742, as a benefit concert.

nodes.name: MIDI standard is agreed
nodes.description: After discussions among instrument makers, the Musical Instrument Digital Interface standard was finalized in 1983, allowing electronic instruments and computers to exchange performance data across manufacturers.

nodes.name: Monterey International Pop Festival takes place
nodes.description: The Monterey International Pop Festival brought a wide-ranging rock, soul, and Indian classical lineup to California in June 1967 and helped turn festival performance into a defining format of the era.

nodes.name: MTV launches
nodes.description: MTV began broadcasting in the United States on 1 August 1981. Its continuous music-video programming made visual presentation a central part of pop promotion and reshaped how artists reached audiences.

nodes.name: Early polyphony is notated in a surviving manuscript
nodes.description: A late-ninth- or early-tenth-century manuscript preserves short notated polyphonic chants, among the earliest surviving written examples of music in more than one part. This evidence documents written transmission, not the beginning of polyphonic practice.

nodes.name: Napster popularizes peer-to-peer music sharing
nodes.description: Napster’s peer-to-peer service made MP3 sharing between personal computers widely visible and challenged established distribution and copyright practices. The service’s legal disputes led to shutdown proceedings in 2001.

nodes.name: Napster suspends its original file-sharing service
nodes.description: After federal court orders in copyright litigation, Napster suspended its original peer-to-peer file-sharing service in 2001. The episode accelerated debate over digital music access, licensing, and online distribution.

nodes.name: Notre-Dame composers develop large-scale polyphony
nodes.description: Composers associated with the Notre-Dame school, including Léonin and Pérotin, developed extended polyphonic settings of liturgical music in late-twelfth-century Paris.

nodes.name: The Original Dixieland Jazz Band records and releases jazz sides
nodes.description: The Original Dixieland Jazz Band recorded and released widely circulated jazz sides for Victor in 1917. “First jazz recording” is a conventional label for this commercially successful release, not proof that earlier Black jazz performance did not exist.

nodes.name: Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo premieres
nodes.description: Claudio Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo was performed at the Gonzaga court in Mantua in 1607 and became one of the earliest operas to remain central to the repertory.

nodes.name: Pansori and Baul songs enter UNESCO’s Representative List
nodes.description: UNESCO incorporated both pansori and Baul songs into its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008. The inscription recognized living traditions and safeguarding needs; it does not date their origins.

nodes.name: Pansori develops in southwest Korea
nodes.description: UNESCO dates pansori’s emergence in southwest Korea to the seventeenth century, probably as a new expression of shamanic narrative songs; the exact beginnings remain uncertain.

nodes.name: Paris Conservatoire is founded
nodes.description: The Conservatoire de Paris was established in 1795 as a state-supported institution for musical training, part of a new model of public music education.

nodes.name: Petrucci prints the Odhecaton
nodes.description: Ottaviano Petrucci publishes Harmonice Musices Odhecaton A in Venice, the first significant printed collection of polyphonic music and a milestone in the wider circulation of written repertory.

nodes.name: The phonautograph traces sound
nodes.description: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville’s phonautograph traces sound waves onto paper but cannot play them back. Its surviving traces were later reconstructed digitally, making it an early milestone in sound recording.

nodes.name: Edison builds the tinfoil phonograph
nodes.description: Thomas Edison’s 1877 tinfoil phonograph recorded and reproduced sound. Later wax-cylinder machines made recorded music practical for commercial distribution.

nodes.name: Renaissance musical exchange reshapes European composition
nodes.description: Circulation among courts, churches, cities, and printers helped spread compositional practices across European regions and supported new secular and sacred repertories. This periodization describes documented exchange, not a single origin.

nodes.name: The Rite of Spring premieres in Paris
nodes.description: Igor Stravinsky’s ballet The Rite of Spring premiered in Paris on 29 May 1913. Its score and staging became a landmark in modern music and dance; accounts of the audience disturbance vary in detail.

nodes.name: Venice opens the Teatro San Cassiano to paying opera audiences
nodes.description: The Teatro San Cassiano opened as a public opera house in Venice in 1637, establishing ticketed opera for paying audiences beyond court and aristocratic settings.

nodes.name: SoundCloud launches audio sharing for creators
nodes.description: SoundCloud was founded in 2007 as a service for creators to upload and share audio, later becoming an important direct-distribution platform for independent and electronic music scenes.

nodes.name: Spotify launches streaming in Europe
nodes.description: Spotify launched in several European markets in October 2008, helping establish on-demand subscription streaming as a major way to access recorded music.

nodes.name: Streaming becomes the leading digital music revenue source in many markets
nodes.description: IFPI reported that streaming revenue overtook download revenue in 37 markets in 2015, reflecting a rapid shift toward access-based listening. The milestone varied by territory and should not be read as a universal crossover date.

nodes.name: TikTok and short-form video reshape music discovery
nodes.description: TikTok’s emergence from Douyin and its later integration with Musical.ly helped make short-form video a major channel for music discovery and user-created circulation. The period is approximate and does not imply that TikTok alone caused viral music trends.

nodes.name: Troubadour song circulates in courtly culture
nodes.description: Troubadours composed and performed vernacular songs, especially in southern French courtly settings. Manuscript survival documents part of a broader performance culture rather than its full extent.

nodes.name: UK Criminal Justice Act targets unlicensed raves
nodes.description: The UK Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 created police powers concerning certain unlicensed gatherings and defined a category of repetitive beats. The law became a major point of conflict around rave culture and public space.

nodes.name: Sony launches the Walkman
nodes.description: Sony launched the TPS-L2 portable cassette player in Japan in July 1979. It reached the United States in June 1980 under the Sound-About name and helped popularize portable headphone listening.

nodes.name: Woodstock Music & Art Fair takes place
nodes.description: The Woodstock Music & Art Fair took place in Bethel, New York, from 15 to 18 August 1969. Its scale, documentation, and later circulation made it a touchstone in the history of rock festivals.

nodes.name: YouTube launches as a public video platform
nodes.description: YouTube’s beta launched in 2005 and the video-sharing site opened more widely later that year. It became a major global channel for music videos, performances, discovery, and fan circulation.

nodes.name: Acid house
nodes.description: A Chicago house style built around the resonant, squelching TB-303 sound, pioneered in recordings by Phuture and other producers. It developed within Chicago’s Black, Latino and gay club cultures, then traveled to Britain through DJs, imported records and clubs, where it helped shape the late-1980s rave movement. “Acid house” also came to name that wider UK scene.

phases.note: Phuture’s “Acid Tracks” circulated by cassette at Ron Hardy’s Music Box before its official 1987 Trax Records pressing; the style and influence predate the commercial release. Chicago origin anchor.
By summer 1988, acid house had spread through British clubs, warehouses and temporary venues. This marks the UK scene’s expansion, not global establishment or the genre’s end.

nodes.phaseNote: These are geographic scene anchors rather than a single global rise-and-fall curve: 1985 marks early Chicago circulation; 1988 marks broad British scene visibility. “Acid house” shifted from a Chicago sound label to a wider UK movement label.

nodes.name: Acid jazz
nodes.description: A British club and recording movement that brought jazz-funk and soul-jazz into dialogue with hip-hop, funk, and dance culture. The term surfaced in London in 1987 and became associated with the Acid Jazz label and artists including the James Taylor Quartet, Brand New Heavies and Jamiroquai. The label and scene continued beyond the 1990s; acid jazz is better treated as a broad, shifting movement than a closed style period.

nodes.name: Afrobeat
nodes.description: Nigerian popular-music style that formed in the Lagos scene of the 1960s–70s, blending West African highlife and rhythmic traditions with American jazz and funk. Fela Kuti and Tony Allen were central, influential figures, though scholarship treats Afrobeat as a scene-based development rather than a single-person invention. Distinct from contemporary Afrobeats.
nodes.phaseNote: Broad scene-era markers, not measured popularity curves: musicology places a nascent Lagos movement in the 1960s–70s, identifies a 1968 public announcement, and documents its institutional consolidation in the early 1970s. Start retained at decade precision because musical formation predates the naming.

nodes.name: Afrobeats
nodes.description: A contested umbrella/category for diverse contemporary West African popular music, with “Afrobeats” also used as a global industry genre label. It is not a single fixed sound and is distinct from Fela Kuti’s earlier Afrobeat. Scholarly work traces the label from West African diasporic circulation to global genre-market use; mainstream North American visibility grew sharply by 2016.
nodes.phaseNote: The source distinguishes an earlier diasporic umbrella term from its mainstream global-category use. 2000 is only a broad start anchor; 2016 is documented North American mainstream visibility, not an origin or peak.

nodes.name: Alternative country
nodes.description: A fluid roots-rock category mixing country song forms and instrumentation with independent rock and punk. Its musical antecedents predate the label; the 1990s scene and press usage crystallized around acts such as Uncle Tupelo.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1990s marker refers to the named scene and category, not the beginning of country-rock crossover. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Alternative rap
nodes.description: A flexible rap category for artists whose approach diverged from dominant commercial conventions through experimental production, lyrical concerns or cross-genre influences. The label is retrospective and overlaps with underground rap and other substyles.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases assigned: “alternative” is a contested, relational label whose meaning changes by scene, period and market context. Available scholarship cautions against treating alternative as a stable sound or universal chronology.

nodes.name: Alternative rock
nodes.description: An umbrella for rock scenes and artists associated with independent labels, college radio and other routes outside mainstream rock; its styles and relation to the mainstream have shifted over time. In the United States, grunge and other acts crossed into mass-market visibility in the early 1990s.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1991 U.S. mainstream crossover is a later milestone, not the genre’s origin or a global popularity peak. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Amapiano
nodes.description: South African township dance music shaped by local house, kwaito and deep-house influences, with sampled percussion, keys and the distinctive log drum. Musicological accounts place its emergence around 2012 in Black townships outside Pretoria and Johannesburg, while stressing contradictory origin stories and many contributors. It gained wider global visibility in the 2020s.
nodes.phaseNote: A 2023 ethnomusicological article dates emergence around 2012 and describes global growth; removed unsupported 2015 “golden age” and 2018 established marker.

nodes.name: Ambient
nodes.description: An umbrella for music foregrounding atmosphere, timbre and space, often with reduced or absent regular beat. Ambient has multiple earlier experimental, psychedelic and environmental strands; Brian Eno named and defined “ambient music” in the liner notes to Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978), rather than inventing every sound later grouped under the term.
nodes.phaseNote: Oxford scholarship situates ambient practices in psychedelic counterculture from the 1960s onward; Cambridge scholarship documents Eno’s 1978 naming/definition. Removed arbitrary 1983 golden-age and 1993 niche/end dates.

nodes.name: Ambient techno
nodes.description: A dance-music formation combining techno/electro rhythmic frameworks with spacious ambient textures.

phases.note: Aphex Twin’s Selected Ambient Works 85–92 and Warp’s Artificial Intelligence series consolidated the style.
The style continued as a listening-oriented strand, for example in Kompakt’s Pop Ambient series.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not measured popularity. The style emerged around 1989 and peaked in the early-to-mid-1990s album era. From the late 1990s, it continued at lower prominence. Boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Americana
nodes.description: A broad, cross-genre American roots category drawing on country, folk, blues, gospel, rock and related traditions. The label became an organized industry category in the 1990s; the music and artists it gathers are older and stylistically diverse.
nodes.phaseNote: No defensible single popularity curve: Americana functions as a broad, cross-genre category, and these sources document industry organization rather than measured genre-wide prominence.

nodes.name: Andean folk
nodes.description: A broad catalogue label for diverse musical practices across the Andes, including Indigenous, folkloric, regional, and popular forms that incorporate these elements. It is not one historically bounded genre; regional and community distinctions matter.
nodes.phaseNote: No single origin date or global prominence curve is supportable for this umbrella label.

nodes.name: Arabic maqam traditions
nodes.description: A family of regional modal systems and performance practices used across Arabic musical traditions. Maqam describes melodic pathways, characteristic phrases and modulation; the timeline start is a cautious documentary-era anchor, not a claim that the tradition began in one year or place.
nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: low. The tradition is a broad family with regional histories; one continuing phase avoids assigning a single prominence peak or flattening those differences. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Bachata
nodes.description: Dominican guitar-based popular music that emerged in marginalized Santo Domingo barrios in the early 1960s from guitar-trio bolero and related Afro-Antillean styles. It developed from music initially described by performers as guitar bolero or campesino bolero; later generations expanded its sound and international reach.
nodes.phaseNote: Peer-reviewed research dates emergence to early 1960s; UNESCO describes its musical and dance expression. Removed unsupported 1975 “golden age” and arbitrary 2010 established date.

nodes.name: Baroque music
nodes.description: Basso continuo, opera, concertos, and contrapuntal invention. Approximate dates mark the historical era, not the disappearance of Baroque performance.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging, not a measured ranking: emergence c. 1600 (monody, early opera), a defining wave from c. 1615 as opera, concerto and sonata spread, consolidation c. 1720, and niche status from c. 1748 as the galant/Classical style displaced it around Bach’s death (1750). Boundaries are approximate; sources support only the c. 1600–1750 era frame.

nodes.name: Baul songs
nodes.description: Devotional songs of Bengal’s Baul communities, joining poetry, melody and embodied spiritual practice. Baul traditions are diverse and transmitted through teacher-disciple relationships; UNESCO traces the songs in Bengali literature to the fifteenth century. The date is a documentary horizon, not a proven point of origin.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed the unsupported single 1800 “established” marker. Literary references and extant song notebooks provide different documentary windows; neither measures a unified popularity cycle.

nodes.name: Bebop
nodes.description: Small-group jazz with fast tempos, intricate melodies, and improvisation over rapidly moving chord changes. A foundational language of modern jazz.

phases.note: Early-1940s Minton’s jam sessions and experiments by Gillespie, Parker, Monk and Clarke.
1945 Parker–Gillespie recordings (“Koko”, “Shaw ’Nuff”); bebop splits jazz in the later 1940s.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: early-1940s emergence and a later-1940s peak are well documented (Britannica, Carnegie Hall); the 1950s “established” phase reflects bop becoming the common modern-jazz vocabulary while hard bop and cool took the spotlight. The 1960 end marks the close of bebop as the leading style, not its disappearance.

nodes.name: Big beat
nodes.description: A UK-led mid-1990s dance movement combining forceful breakbeats, sampled hooks, rock-scale dynamics, and rave energy. Its category boundaries overlap with breaks and alternative dance; its prominence as a named scene later receded, while musical influence continued.
nodes.phaseNote: The named movement coalesced around 1995–96, achieved late-1990s crossover success and later lost some commercial momentum; this does not establish an end to the style. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Black metal
nodes.description: An extreme-metal genre family with distinct waves and regional scenes. Venom’s 1982 album supplied the name; the Norwegian second wave of the early 1990s later shaped a particularly influential sound and public image.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1982 marker refers to the naming/first-wave anchor, not the whole genre’s invention. The early-1990s phase marks the well-documented Norwegian second wave and wider recognition, not a universal popularity ranking.

nodes.name: Bluegrass
nodes.description: An acoustic string-band genre shaped by Bill Monroe and the Blue Grass Boys, drawing on older Appalachian and country traditions. Earl Scruggs’s 1945 arrival helped crystallize the classic ensemble and three-finger banjo style.
nodes.phaseNote: 1945 marks the documented crystallization of the classic ensemble, not an exact invention date. The 1970s marker reflects documented festival, label, and radio proliferation; phases are historical editorial cues, not measured popularity rankings.

nodes.name: Blues
nodes.description: African American musical traditions shaped by expressive vocal phrasing, blue notes, and recurring harmonic forms. A major source for jazz, rhythm and blues, and rock and roll.

phases.note: Carnegie Hall’s timeline dates blues as a recognizable genre in the Deep South to the 1890s.
From 1920 record companies recorded vaudeville and then rural blues, and blues records were heavily marketed through the 1920s.
Amplified Chicago blues flourished in the 1950s, but Smithsonian Folkways describes blues fading from wider popular memory early in the decade before a late-1950s/1960s revival.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging: emergence as a recognizable genre in the 1890s, the 1920s recording boom that made blues a mass-market style, then continued practice from the 1950s (Chicago electric blues, revival audiences) without implying a measured peak. Shading is approximate, not a popularity ranking.

nodes.name: Blues rock
nodes.description: A rock-blues fusion using amplified electric-blues vocabulary, rock rhythms and often extended guitar-led improvisation. It emerged in the 1960s and has continued in multiple forms.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases assigned: the graph’s prior 1963, 1968 and 1973 milestones and 1975 endpoint were not tied to a defensible genre-wide evidence base. Blues-rock activity continued beyond the 1970s.

nodes.name: Boom bap
nodes.description: A sample-based East Coast hip-hop production aesthetic associated with hard, swung kick-and-snare patterns, chopped loops and an emphasis on drum breaks. It remains a reference point for later production rather than a closed historical genre.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases assigned. Scholarly work traces boom bap to the late 1980s and treats it as a continuing production reference; the graph’s 1991 golden-age and 1996 niche labels were unsupported.

nodes.name: Bossa nova
nodes.description: A Brazilian song style that took shape in late-1950s Rio de Janeiro through a distinctive samba-derived guitar approach, understated vocals, and jazz-influenced harmony. Several 1958 recordings are cited as early turning points, so no single uncontested “birth” recording is claimed.
nodes.phaseNote: Late-1950s emergence is supported, but the precise first recording is disputed. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Breakbeat
nodes.description: A broad rhythmic and production approach built around syncopated drum breaks, sampled, looped, or programmed. The term spans hip-hop, UK rave, jungle, big beat and later dance scenes rather than describing one bounded genre.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases assigned because breakbeat names a wide rhythmic lineage across scenes and decades. The earlier single golden-age phase and 1996 endpoint confused a broad technique/family with a bounded genre.

nodes.name: Breakbeat hardcore
nodes.phaseNote: UK rave-scene visibility was concentrated in the early 1990s, and the broad hardcore category fragmented into related branches by 1993. No complete prominence curve is assigned.
nodes.description: An early-1990s UK rave style combining house and acid-house structures with chopped breakbeats, sampling, and influences circulating through hip-hop and sound-system culture. As the rave scene fragmented, related strands developed into jungle, darkcore, and happy hardcore.

nodes.name: Breakcore
nodes.description: An experimental electronic music category built around chopped, distorted and rapidly rearranged breakbeats, associated with hardcore, jungle and noise; its boundaries remain fluid and artists vary widely.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases assigned: the 2001 “golden age” and 2018 established labels had no substantiated evidence, and breakcore is a dispersed, artist-led category without a single consensus peak.

nodes.name: Britpop
nodes.description: A British 1990s guitar-pop movement and press category, associated with melodic songwriting and British cultural references. Its boundaries and representation were contested; the 1995 Blur–Oasis chart battle marks a documented high-visibility moment, not a complete definition of the scene.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1990s mark a broad category emergence, while 1995 is a UK press and chart-visibility milestone rather than the end of activity. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Calypso
nodes.description: A Trinidadian song tradition closely tied to Carnival, shaped by Afro-Trinidadian performance and known for topical lyrics, social commentary, and competitive singing. The word “calypso” is documented around 1900, but the musical tradition predates that label; its exact early chronology remains difficult to establish.
nodes.phaseNote: No single measured prominence curve is defensible from the sources reviewed. 1900 is a term/documentation marker, not a musical birth date; 1914 marks the first commercial recording cited by the national library.

nodes.name: Carnatic music
nodes.description: The South Indian classical system, with distinct regional histories, performance lineages and approaches to melody and rhythm. The date is an approximate modern-era anchor, not a claim of origin.
nodes.phaseNote: A single continuing phase is used because this broad, long-running tradition does not have a defensible shared peak cycle in the current graph sources. Shading is editorial, not a measured ranking; regional histories may require separate phases.

nodes.name: Chicago house
nodes.description: A Chicago house style and club practice that emerged in late-1970s and 1980s Black and queer nightlife, including The Warehouse and Music Box. DJs reworked disco, funk, and electronic recordings with edits and drum machines; the precise origin of the word “house” remains disputed.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1980s marker describes Chicago scene formation, not a measured global popularity history. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Chillwave
nodes.description: A late-2000s/early-2010s online scene and style built around hazy production, reverb, softened vocals and nostalgic pop textures, overlapping with dream pop and synth-pop.
nodes.phaseNote: The chillwave label appeared in online music writing around 2009; later influence should not be mistaken for a firm genre endpoint. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Chopped and screwed
nodes.description: A Houston DJ style that slows recordings and reshapes them through repeated cuts, creating a heavy, suspended feel. DJ Screw developed it in a local mixtape culture that also gave MCs space to freestyle over the mixes.
nodes.phaseNote: DJ Screw developed the technique in the early 1990s, with a documented breakthrough in 1993; national recognition followed later. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Classical era
nodes.description: The Classical period, not the umbrella term classical music: balanced phrases, sonata form, symphonies, and string quartets. Its historical boundaries overlap the Romantic era.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging, not a measured ranking: emergence c. 1750 (galant and early symphony), a defining wave from c. 1764 (Haydn at Esterháza, Mozart’s early maturity), consolidation c. 1806 as Beethoven’s middle period bridges toward Romanticism, and niche status from c. 1818. Boundaries are approximate and overlap the Romantic era.

nodes.name: Congolese rumba
nodes.description: Urban music from the Congos shaped through exchange with Afro-Cuban records and local musical practice. Its later branches include soukous; the timeline start marks its documented emergence in the 1940s, not the deeper history of its component traditions.

phases.note: Rumba Lingala emerged in Congolese urban centers in the 1940s; scholarship documents locally recorded music by 1948. The specific label and boundaries are not uniform across sources.
Congolese orchestras and recordings expanded through the 1950s–60s; sources differ on whether this is the genre’s origin or a major consolidation of an earlier urban style.

nodes.phaseNote: These broad stages distinguish 1940s urban emergence from 1950s–60s orchestral expansion, not a measured popularity curve. Removed unsupported 1970 and 2000 “established” markers; later practice and UNESCO recognition are not an end date.

nodes.name: Conscious hip-hop
nodes.description: Rap that foregrounds social analysis, self-knowledge, political critique or community concerns. Its boundaries overlap with political rap and other styles, and artists do not always embrace the label.
nodes.phaseNote: No phase boundaries retained: the label is contested, socially conscious content overlaps with broader rap history, and the proposed 1997 and 2018 markers were not established as genre-wide transitions by the sources reviewed.

nodes.name: Contemporary R&B
nodes.description: A broad modern R&B style shaped by studio production, soul vocals and exchange with hip-hop and pop. Its sound changes over time, so this node is an umbrella rather than one fixed formula.

phases.note: Carnegie Hall traces post-disco diversification of Black popular music and new label debates from the late 1970s into the 1980s.
Billboard reintroduced “R&B” as an umbrella chart term in 1990, and hip-hop-inflected R&B production became standard through the 1990s and 2000s.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging: 1980s emergence of post-disco, studio-built R&B; a high-visibility era from the 1990 R&B relabelling through the hip-hop-blended 1990s–2000s; continuing activity later. The 2018 marker is a provisional editorial estimate, not a measured popularity shift.

nodes.name: Cool jazz
nodes.description: Restrained dynamics, lighter timbres, and carefully arranged textures in postwar jazz. Includes, but is not synonymous with, West Coast jazz.

phases.note: Late-1940s emergence; Davis’s Birth of the Cool sessions (1949–50).
Early-to-mid-1950s West Coast recording boom (Mulligan quartet 1952, Brubeck).

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: cool jazz emerges in the late 1940s and its publicity peak is the early–middle-1950s West Coast scene (Britannica, Carnegie Hall); the late-1950s phase reflects hard bop and modal jazz overtaking it. Boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Country
nodes.description: A US popular tradition shaped by rural string-band music, balladry, blues and regional performance circuits; its commercial forms include honky-tonk, bluegrass, country-pop and many others.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1920s marker refers to the commercial recording category, not the beginning of the older regional traditions that shaped country music. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Crunk
nodes.description: Southern hip-hop and club-rap style associated especially with Atlanta, built around heavy bass, shouted ad-libs, chants, and call-and-response. Its roots overlap earlier regional bass and club traditions, making a precise origin contested; Lil Jon and the East Side Boyz helped carry its sound into mainstream hip-hop in the early 2000s.

phases.note: The exact origin is not datable: “crunk” circulated in Southern rap and club scenes before it became a distinct, marketed subgenre. The decade is a broad roots marker.
Lil Jon & the East Side Boyz’ Kings of Crunk (2002) and early-2000s crossover successes mark the major national prominence wave.
The mainstream wave shifted toward snap and trap, but crunk’s sound persisted and diversified; this is not a genre endpoint.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate editorial arc: regional roots during the 1990s, a national prominence wave around 2002–04, then continued influence as mainstream Southern rap shifted toward snap and trap. “Established” signals persistence, not measured popularity or decline to a niche.

nodes.name: Cumbia
nodes.description: Afro-Indigenous rooted music, dance, and social practice of Colombia’s Caribbean coast, especially the Bajo Magdalena, with many local and transnational forms. Sources distinguish this older community tradition from cumbia’s emergence as a Colombian commercial music category in the 1940s and its later spread across Latin America.

nodes.name: Dancehall
nodes.description: Jamaican music and performance culture that developed from sound-system dances and deejay performance. The Jamaican government’s heritage account traces deejaying to the 1970s, blossoming in the 1980s, and describes dancehall as both a place and the music; scholarly accounts trace the wider sound-system culture further back. Digital riddim production became a defining shift in 1985.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial phases distinguish the 1970s rise of dancehall deejaying, the 1985 digital riddim watershed, and early-1990s international diffusion. “Golden-age” here denotes a stylistic watershed, not a measured popularity peak; the 1990s boundary is broad and confidence is low.

nodes.name: Darksynth
nodes.description: A synthwave subgenre associated with darker horror and cyberpunk imagery and heavier metal, industrial, or post-punk inflections. The label overlaps with dark synthwave and related microgenres, so its boundaries and exact emergence date remain provisional.

nodes.name: Death metal
nodes.description: An extreme metal genre that coalesced from thrash and related underground styles in the mid-1980s. Early scenes in the United States, followed by distinct Florida and Swedish centers, developed through tape trading; the style later diversified into multiple overlapping subgenres.
nodes.phaseNote: The graph uses decade-level origin for the genre’s early- to mid-1980s formation. The 1989–93 commercial golden age is directly stated by Chaker and Kahn-Harris; the 1995 established marker is a cautious editorial stage for the post-peak era and diversification, not a return to measured popularity.

nodes.name: Deep house
nodes.description: A house subgenre that emerged from Chicago’s underground in the 1980s, blending house with jazz-funk, soul and disco influences. Larry Heard’s early recordings are foundational, while later Chicago, New Jersey, and international scenes shaped its sound and audience.
nodes.phaseNote: Early Chicago scene development in the 1980s and a defining early-to-mid-1990s period are documented, without establishing a global popularity peak or later niche boundary. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Detroit techno
nodes.description: A regional form of techno developed by Detroit-area artists from the early to mid-1980s. Its history includes the Belleville Three, other Detroit producers and labels, Black radio and club culture, and exchanges with Chicago and Europe.

phases.note: Early Cybotron releases provide a recorded milestone for a scene with earlier roots.
A UK compilation and the Music Institute mark international exposure; the second wave followed from about 1989.
After the first and second waves, Detroit became one hub in a global techno network. A 1995 third-wave compilation and the festival founded in 2000 show continuing activity.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not measured popularity. Emergence starts with Cybotron around 1981. A peak from 1988 covers international exposure and the second wave. Established activity from 1995 reflects the third wave and the DEMF/Movement era. The 1995 boundary is approximate.

nodes.name: Disco
nodes.phaseNote: U.S. disco reached mainstream prominence in the mid-1970s, faced a backlash in 1979 and continued in underground scenes. Later revivals and global histories cannot be represented by one supported curve. No complete prominence curve is assigned.
nodes.description: A dance-music family shaped in 1970s club networks, especially in New York and Philadelphia, by Black, Latino, and LGBTQ communities and by producers working across soul, funk, and orchestral pop. Club DJ practice, extended mixes, and the 12-inch single became important to its circulation; its histories continued after the U.S. backlash of 1979.

nodes.name: Doo-wop
nodes.description: A vocal-group style built around close harmonies, syllabic backing vocals and a prominent lead singer, flourishing in the 1950s and early 1960s.

phases.note: The Orioles’ “It’s Too Soon to Know” (1948) set the romantic vocal-group model that many “bird” groups emulated.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging: late-1940s emergence of R&B vocal-harmony groups, a mid-1950s to early-1960s peak of doo-wop hits, then niche status as the style faded from the charts in the early 1960s. Boundaries are approximate and not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Doom metal
nodes.description: A slow, weighty metal style rooted in Black Sabbath’s early-1970s sound and shaped into a distinct underground genre by Sabbath-influenced bands in the late 1970s and 1980s. “Doom metal” became common as a label by the mid-1980s; its later branches include death/doom, stoner, sludge and drone metal.

nodes.name: Downtempo
nodes.description: A broad label for low-tempo electronic dance and listening music, including distinct forms such as ambient, ambient dub, chill-out, ambient house, chill hop and trip hop. These styles have different lineages; “downtempo” describes an overlapping umbrella rather than a single unified genre history.

nodes.name: Dream pop
nodes.description: An atmospheric pop and rock style that gives sonic texture weight alongside melody, often using soft or breathy vocals and effects-treated guitars or synthesizers. It emerged from 1980s British post-punk and new wave, with Cocteau Twins among its central early reference points; it overlaps with but is not synonymous with shoegaze.

nodes.name: Drill
nodes.description: A rap subgenre that emerged from Chicago’s underground hip-hop scene in the early 2010s and entered wider U.S. visibility through artists including Chief Keef. Distinct regional forms developed later, including UK drill, which spread in London from the mid-to-late 2010s; the name covers related but locally distinct sounds.

nodes.name: Drum and bass
nodes.description: A UK electronic dance genre that emerged from early-1990s London rave and club culture through the jungle/breakbeat continuum. It centers fast, chopped breakbeats and bass, shaped in part by Jamaican sound-system culture and Black Atlantic musical practice. “Jungle” and “drum and bass” overlap historically but are not always interchangeable labels.

nodes.name: Dub
nodes.description: A Jamaican reggae genre and studio practice that emerged from late-1960s sound-system “versioning” and developed into a distinct form in the early 1970s. Engineers use the mixing desk as an instrument, reshaping existing recordings through subtraction, bass and drum emphasis, echo, reverb and other effects. Dub techniques later traveled widely and were absorbed into other genres.

nodes.name: Dub techno
nodes.description: A techno and dub synthesis associated especially with Berlin’s Basic Channel releases in the early 1990s. Long delays, reverberation, filtering, and reduced rhythmic material make space and decay part of the composition.

phases.note: Basic Channel’s first 12-inch singles in Berlin.
The BCD compilation became the style’s defining document.
A second generation, including Deepchord and Echospace, kept the style current.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not measured popularity. Basic Channel releases from 1993 set the template, followed by a mid-to-late-1990s peak. From 2000, later producers continued the style. Boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Dubstep
nodes.description: A UK electronic dance genre that emerged in early-2000s South London from darker strains of garage and two-step, with sparse rhythms, sub-bass, and influences from Jamaican sound-system and dubplate culture. It rapidly developed transnationally; the later North American commercial form changed its sound, so Croydon origins do not describe the whole genre.

nodes.name: East Coast rap
nodes.description: A regional umbrella for rap and hip-hop scenes associated with New York and the broader U.S. East Coast. It grew distinct as hip-hop regionalized in the 1980s, with styles varying across artists, cities and generations; the East/West identity became especially market-visible in the 1990s.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed unsupported 1975 origin, 1990 “golden age,” and 2010 establishment phases. Sources describe regionalization and a 1990s East/West market distinction, not a measurable coast-wide popularity curve.

nodes.name: EDM
nodes.description: In North American music-industry usage, “EDM” became a catch-all label in the late 2000s for dance and club electronic music, especially commercially oriented festival sounds. It is a broad marketing category overlapping house, trance and other styles, not one stable musical form or the origin of electronic dance music.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed the unsupported 2008 golden-age and 2018 established phases. Available sources support the term’s late-2000s uptake and festival-market association, not a single popularity curve for the umbrella category.

nodes.name: Electro
nodes.description: A Black American electronic dance and hip-hop style associated with drum-machine rhythms, synthesized bass and vocoders. Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force’s 1982 “Planet Rock” is widely treated as a foundational electro recording; electro continued beyond its early-1980s breakthrough and developed regional offshoots.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed the unsupported 1990 end date and narrow golden-age phase. 1982 is a landmark recording date, not the invention of electronic dance music or the end of electro.

nodes.name: Electro house
nodes.description: A 2000s house branch combining house rhythms with prominent electro-influenced synth timbres and forceful production.
nodes.phaseNote: No prominence phases retained. Available sources document electro-house as a 2000s production/scene category but do not establish a measured genre-wide peak or decline.

nodes.name: Electroclash
nodes.description: A turn-of-the-millennium club scene combining electro, synth-pop/new wave references, punk attitude and theatrical performance; also a press and nightlife label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate late-1990s emergence and early-2000s visibility; this reflects an identifiable club/press scene, not a measured peak or the disappearance of related electro-pop styles.

nodes.name: Emo
nodes.description: A shifting family of rock styles usually traced to 1980s Washington, DC hardcore and later independent scenes. The label has been disputed by musicians and applied to distinct later waves; some emo-associated bands reached broad mainstream visibility in the early 2000s.
nodes.phaseNote: These broad anchors distinguish the contested 1980s DC lineage from early-2000s mainstream visibility; they do not describe one continuous sound or an end date. Removed the unsupported 1993 “golden age” and 2003 niche phase.

nodes.name: Folk revival
nodes.description: The twentieth-century folk-revival tradition represented here centers on vernacular song, singer-songwriters and revival performance in the United States and Britain; it does not stand for every traditional music worldwide.

phases.note: Lomax's Library of Congress recordings of Guthrie and the Almanac Singers (1941) seed the revival.
The Weavers' 1950 hit 'Goodnight, Irene' makes revival folk a commercial pop phenomenon.
Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' (1958), Newport 1959 and Baez/Dylan drive the boom to its mid-1960s peak.
The commercial boom recedes into folk-rock and singer-songwriter currents; revival performance continues.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: 1930s roots (Library of Congress field recordings, Guthrie, Almanac Singers), a 1950 commercial breakthrough with the Weavers, a 1958–mid-1960s boom, then continuing but less central activity. Replaces an unsupported 1945–2010 golden age.

nodes.name: Juke / footwork
